raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old woman with no underlying comorbidities presented to our unit with progressively worsening left-sided pelvic pain, especially when walking.
At the first presentation to our unit 5 years ago, she had been initially referred to us by our gynaecology colleagues after a workup for a long-standing history of pelvic pain revealed a 7.5 x 6.7 x 8.8 cm [transverse (TV) x anteroposterior (AP) x craniocaudal (CC)] multiloculated cystic lesion in the left iliac fossa on computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis (Figure 1). The lesion extended posteriorly, involving the gluteus medius muscle and notable destruction of the left iliac wing bone. Percutaneous biopsy of the cystic mass revealed histopathology consistent with hydatid disease. Therefore, a tentative diagnosis of primary pelvic bone hydatid disease was made. Preoperative albendazole was given, and it was decided to proceed with surgical exploration to excise the cystic lesion. Unfortunately, due to poor social circumstances, the patient defaulted on follow-up.
She now re-presented to our department 4 years later with worsening left-sided pelvic pain impeding her ability to weight-bear. She had also noted that her initial left pelvic mass had increased in size compared with 4 years ago and that there was another enlarging mass noted over the left posterior gluteal area. Physical examination revealed a 10 x 14 cm fixed, nontender, firm mass in the left iliac fossa. In addition, another 5 x 5 cm was found in the left superior gluteal region. Laboratory workup, including CA125, was unremarkable. Repeat CT showed a large thick-walled multicystic lesion in the left lower pelvis extending posteriorly into the gluteus muscle (Figure 2). Imaging also revealed significant lytic change within the left iliac bone resulting in extensive bony destruction of the left iliac wing and involvement of the sacroiliac joint (Figure 3).
A decision was made at the multidisciplinary team meeting, including an orthopaedic surgeon and social worker, to surgically explore and debulk the lesion to relieve painful pressure effects of the hydatid, cystic mass and prevent further disease progression. An orthopaedic consultation advised that major pelvic bone reconstruction would not be possible. Due to the extensive left iliac wing destruction and involvement of the sacroiliac joint, complete excision would not be possible without causing significant disability to the patient postoperatively.
After a 14-day course of preoperative albendazole therapy, she was taken to theatre. A left anterior iliac crest incision was made. Operative findings revealed a large extraperitoneal multicystic lesion containing thick hydatid sand and multiple daughter cysts. Sterile swabs soaked in scolicidal agent (0.1% sodium hypochlorite solution) were placed around the cystic operative field (Figure 4). Extraperitoneal excision of the multicystic lesion was performed. The extraperitoneal cavity and bony fragments from the pelvic wing that were visualised intraoperatively were also debrided (Figure 5). The cystic cavity was then irrigated with a scolicidal agent, followed by saline. The cavity was closed with closed suction drains left in place. Histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of the left pelvic bone and soft tissue hydatid disease.
The postoperative period was uneventful. A small discharging sinus at the incision site settled with gentle saline irrigation. On follow-up, a month later, her pain symptoms had largely resolved, and she was walking with much less difficulty and able to weight-bear. She continued albendazole therapy for 6 months postsurgery and remained asymptomatic throughout.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old woman presented with progressively worsening left-sided pelvic pain impairing ambulation and enlarging left iliac fossa and left gluteal masses 4 years after defaulting on treatment for pelvic bone hydatid disease.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Five years prior to current admission, a CT scan and percutaneous biopsy for chronic pelvic pain had established a diagnosis of primary left iliac bone hydatid disease (7.5 x 6.7 x 8.8 cm cyst), and she received preoperative albendazole before defaulting on surgical follow-up. She re-presented 4 years later with severe left pelvic pain preventing weight-bearing, enlargement of the left iliac fossa mass, and a new left posterior gluteal swelling.
subjective.past_medical_history: Biopsy-proven left pelvic bone hydatid disease diagnosed 5 years earlier; no other medical comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for worsening left pelvic pain, gait impairment, and enlarging left pelvic and gluteal masses.

objective.physical_examination: A fixed, firm, non-tender 10 x 14 cm mass was palpated in the left iliac fossa accompanied by a second 5 x 5 cm mass in the left superior gluteal region.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood workup and serum CA-125 were unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial abdominopelvic CT (5 years prior) showed a 7.5 x 6.7 x 8.8 cm multiloculated left iliac fossa cyst eroding the left iliac wing and gluteus medius, confirmed as hydatid disease on percutaneous biopsy. Repeat CT at re-presentation demonstrated a large thick-walled multicystic pelvic lesion extending into the gluteal musculature with extensive osteolytic destruction of the left iliac wing and sacroiliac joint involvement. Following 14 days of preoperative albendazole, extraperitoneal surgical debulking and bone debridement via a left anterior iliac crest incision (with 0.1% sodium hypochlorite scolicidal packing and irrigation) evacuated thick hydatid sand and multiple daughter cysts; histopathology reconfirmed pelvic osseous and soft-tissue hydatid disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Extensive primary left iliac bone, sacroiliac joint, and gluteal soft-tissue cystic echinococcosis, confirmed by percutaneous biopsy, intraoperative extraction of daughter cysts and hydatid sand, and postoperative histopathology. Managed with 14 days of preoperative oral albendazole, extraperitoneal surgical debulking, osseous debridement, 0.1% sodium hypochlorite irrigation, and 6 months of postoperative albendazole, achieving marked pain relief and restoration of weight-bearing ambulation.
